items.prompt: A Kinesis Data Stream throttles producers during a predictable peak. What capacity decision should be evaluated?
constraints: Record rate and size are measured.

options.text: Calculate shard or on-demand capacity from write bytes, records, partition-key distribution, and peak headroom, then scale before the peak and monitor throttling.
Add consumers because consumer count increases producer write capacity automatically.
Use one constant partition key so all shards share the same ordering.
Retry writes without backoff until the stream accepts them.

feedback.Reason: Kinesis producer capacity depends on shard or mode limits and partition-key distribution, not consumer count alone.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A shard has write record and byte limits; partition keys map records to shards and can create hot shards.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect models peak payloads and keys, scales ahead of demand, and uses backoff for transient throttles.
Details.errorCorrection: Consumers do not add write capacity, one key concentrates load, and tight retries amplify throttling.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Pre-scaling costs more but protects freshness and avoids producer rejection during a known peak.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Read capacity does not increase producer shard write capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A constant key concentrates all records in one shard.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Backoff is required to avoid an amplification loop.

items.prompt: Most events use the same tenant key and one Kinesis shard is hot while other shards are idle. What pattern should be considered?
constraints: The hot tenant can fan out reads.

options.text: Use a bounded write-sharding suffix or a better distribution key while preserving the tenant identity for downstream aggregation and documenting ordering changes.
Increase consumer count because it redistributes producer partition keys.
Keep the hot key and add shards because a key is automatically rehashed on every write.
Drop hot-tenant records until the shard catches up.

feedback.Reason: Partition-key choice controls shard distribution; sharding a hot logical key trades strict per-key order for throughput.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Kinesis uses the partition key to select a shard; a deterministic suffix can spread one logical tenant across shards.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner aggregates shards downstream and makes the loss of strict tenant ordering explicit if acceptable.
Details.errorCorrection: Consumers do not rehash producer writes, adding shards does not split an unchanged hot key, and dropping records loses data.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Write sharding improves throughput but requires fan-out and a new ordering contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Consumer scale does not change producer key routing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: An unchanged partition key continues to select the same shard range.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Data loss is not a throughput remediation.

items.prompt: A Kinesis consumer has growing iterator age even after adding more application workers. What should be checked?

options.text: Correlate shard count, consumer lease distribution, worker limits, record processing time, downstream latency, and checkpoint behavior before adding capacity.
Add unlimited workers because every worker reads every shard independently without coordination.
Increase producer rate so consumers receive more parallel work.
Reset all checkpoints to trim iterator age without verifying record processing.

feedback.Reason: Consumer lag depends on shard parallelism, lease distribution, processing rate, checkpoints, and downstream capacity.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A consumer application assigns shard work to workers and advances checkpoints after processing; shard count limits natural parallelism.
Details.scenarioApplication: The operator identifies whether workers are idle, overloaded, unevenly leased, or blocked downstream.
Details.errorCorrection: Unbounded workers do not create shard parallelism, more producer load worsens lag, and resetting checkpoints risks data loss or duplication.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More workers can reduce lag until shard or downstream limits are reached, at additional cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Consumer parallelism is bounded by shards and lease coordination.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: More input increases backlog when consumers are already behind.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Checkpoint changes can skip or duplicate records and are not a lag fix.

items.prompt: A Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream sends data to S3 and the business accepts up to five-minute delivery latency. Which settings matter?
constraints: Freshness and object size are both relevant.

options.text: Tune Firehose buffering size and interval, compression or format conversion, partitioning, error output, and destination capacity against the freshness and object-size objectives.
Set an infinite buffer because Firehose guarantees immediate delivery after any amount of data accumulates.
Use Firehose as a random-access transactional database for each record.
Disable buffering because S3 accepts only one record per object.

feedback.Reason: Firehose batches records for delivery and its buffer hints trade delivery latency against object efficiency and destination load.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Firehose buffers records by size or time before delivering to destinations and can transform or compress them.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner selects buffering from freshness and downstream query layout and monitors delivery failures and age.
Details.errorCorrection: Infinite buffering violates freshness, Firehose is not transactional random access, and S3 supports objects containing many records.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Larger buffers improve object and request efficiency but delay delivery and increase loss scope before flush.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An unbounded buffer would violate a freshness objective.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Firehose is a delivery service, not a transactional record store.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Buffering is central to efficient Firehose delivery to S3.

items.prompt: Athena queries need events partitioned by tenant and event date as Firehose delivers to S3. Which feature should be evaluated?
constraints: Partition fields are in each record.
The S3 prefix can be generated.

options.text: Use Firehose dynamic partitioning or an equivalent delivery-prefix design, validating key extraction, small-file behavior, buffering, and late-arriving records.
Write every event to one prefix because Athena partition pruning ignores object prefixes.
Create one Firehose delivery stream per tenant without estimating stream count and cost.
Use a cache key as the S3 partition path without storing the event fields needed for replay.

feedback.Reason: Partitioned S3 prefixes reduce scan cost when delivery can derive stable partition keys from records.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Firehose can use record fields to construct dynamic S3 prefixes; Athena and other engines can prune partitions from predicates.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect balances partition cardinality, object size, late data, and catalog updates.
Details.errorCorrection: A single prefix prevents pruning, one stream per tenant can exceed operational scale, and cache keys are not a replay contract.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Fine partitions lower scan volume but can create many small files and catalog overhead.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Object prefixes are a key input to partition pruning in a lake layout.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Per-tenant streams multiply quotas and operations without necessity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Partition paths need durable source fields and should not depend on ephemeral cache state.

items.prompt: A Firehose Lambda transformation fails for malformed records. What delivery behavior should be designed?

options.text: Configure transformation failure handling and an error prefix, emit failure metadata, monitor retry and backup behavior, and preserve the source for corrected replay.
Return success for malformed records so Firehose deletes them from the stream.
Retry the same malformed record forever without a dead-letter or alarm path.
Drop the entire delivery stream whenever one transformation fails.

feedback.Reason: Transformation errors need a visible, bounded recovery path that does not silently lose good or bad data.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Firehose can invoke a transformation and deliver failed records or error output according to configured behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner inspects error records, fixes the transformation, and replays from durable source data.
Details.errorCorrection: Success discards or mislabels failures, infinite retries block progress, and stopping all delivery is disproportionate without an explicit outage policy.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Error backup consumes storage but makes data-quality remediation possible.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Returning success for malformed data can lose the record or hide corruption.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Retry loops need limits and an error destination.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: One malformed record should not necessarily block every valid record.

items.prompt: An organization already operates Kafka producers and needs managed brokers while retaining Kafka APIs and partition semantics. Which service should be evaluated?
constraints: The team wants broker management reduced.

options.text: Evaluate Amazon MSK with compatible Kafka versions, broker and storage sizing, partition distribution, networking, security, retention, and client migration testing.
Use Firehose because it is a drop-in Kafka broker for arbitrary consumer groups.
Use S3 as a Kafka topic because objects preserve consumer offsets automatically.
Replace Kafka with DynamoDB streams without mapping partition and retention behavior.

feedback.Reason: MSK provides managed Kafka-compatible infrastructure when Kafka APIs and operational semantics are required.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: MSK runs open-source Apache Kafka or compatible options with brokers, topics, partitions, replication, and consumer groups.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect verifies client compatibility, subnet and security configuration, storage growth, and partition leadership.
Details.errorCorrection: Firehose is a delivery service, S3 is not a Kafka broker, and DynamoDB Streams has different partition, retention, and consumer semantics.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: MSK reduces broker operations but leaves Kafka capacity, partition, client, and application responsibilities.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Firehose does not provide Kafka broker and consumer-group semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 objects do not implement Kafka offsets and partition consumers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A service migration requires semantic mapping, not a name substitution.

items.prompt: An MSK topic has uneven partition traffic and consumers cannot keep up with one partition. What should be reviewed?

options.text: Review partition-key distribution, partition count, leader and broker balance, consumer assignment, message size, and the migration or reassignment impact of adding partitions.
Add consumer instances only because consumers can split one hot partition arbitrarily.
Use one partition so all events are globally ordered and throughput increases.
Delete the topic and recreate it whenever a partition becomes hot.

feedback.Reason: Kafka scale follows partition distribution and consumer assignment; a hot partition remains a bottleneck until the key model changes.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Kafka consumers process partitions, and a partition's ordering and throughput are bounded independently of the topic total.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner chooses a new key or repartitioning strategy and tests consumer lag and ordering implications.
Details.errorCorrection: Consumers cannot split one partition's ordered stream arbitrarily, one partition limits scale, and deletion destroys retained data.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More partitions increase parallelism but can affect ordering, metadata, and operational overhead.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Consumer count cannot split a single ordered partition beyond its assignment semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: One partition sacrifices throughput and parallelism.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Topic deletion is destructive and not a capacity strategy.

items.prompt: An MSK cluster must keep topic data available after a broker failure. Which design should be checked?

options.text: Use appropriate replication factor and in-sync replica settings across AZs, configure producer acknowledgments, and test broker failure, leader election, and recovery capacity.
Use replication factor one because the managed broker is itself a backup.
Place every broker in one AZ to reduce replication latency regardless of availability.
Disable acknowledgments because replication makes producer durability automatic.

feedback.Reason: Kafka durability depends on replicated partitions, in-sync replicas, acknowledgment policy, and failure-domain placement.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Topic replicas across brokers and AZs can elect a leader after failure; producer acknowledgment determines when writes are considered accepted.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests loss of broker and AZ capacity and verifies that producers and consumers recover without violating retention or durability goals.
Details.errorCorrection: Managed broker is not a data replica, one AZ shares failure, and disabled acknowledgments weaken durability signals.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Higher replication consumes storage and network but improves failure tolerance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A broker failure can lose a partition without replicas.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: One AZ creates a shared failure domain.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Acknowledgment policy remains part of the producer durability contract.

items.prompt: Only private application subnets should publish to an MSK cluster. Which network design fits?
constraints: Security groups can reference client groups.

options.text: Place MSK brokers in private subnets across AZs and allow only required client security groups and Kafka ports, with DNS, routes, and TLS or auth validated.
Expose brokers publicly because Kafka clients need direct access to every broker address.
Allow the entire internet to Kafka ports and rely on topic ACLs alone.
Use a NAT gateway as a Kafka broker endpoint for private clients.

feedback.Reason: MSK uses private VPC networking and broker-level client reachability must be constrained by routes and security controls.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Kafka clients discover broker endpoints and need network access to the broker ports through private VPC paths.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect validates client DNS and security-group rules for every broker and AZ.
Details.errorCorrection: Public exposure is unnecessary, ACLs do not replace network protection, and NAT is not a broker endpoint.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Private networking requires route and client configuration but reduces attack surface.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Private broker access is the intended MSK network model for internal clients.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Topic ACLs do not justify broad network exposure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: NAT gateways translate egress and do not provide Kafka broker discovery.

items.prompt: An MSK topic retention policy causes broker storage to approach its limit. What should be reviewed?
constraints: The cluster can be resized or rebalanced.

options.text: Model ingestion rate, message size, replication factor, retention, broker storage headroom, partition distribution, and scaling or archiving options before storage exhaustion.
Delete old data immediately without checking the retention contract or consumer offsets.
Add consumers because more consumers reduce broker storage usage automatically.
Increase replication factor to create more free storage on each broker.

feedback.Reason: Kafka storage grows from payload rate, retention, and replication and needs proactive capacity modeling.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Each broker stores partition replicas for the retention period; replication increases stored bytes and traffic.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner sets alarms and headroom and changes retention or capacity only with consumer and compliance analysis.
Details.errorCorrection: Deleting data may violate retention, consumers read but do not delete broker storage independently, and replication increases storage usage.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Long retention supports replay but costs storage; archive or tiering can reduce broker pressure if semantics permit.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Retention is a business and recovery requirement, not an arbitrary cleanup lever.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Consumer progress does not automatically remove retained log segments before policy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Higher replication consumes more storage rather than creating free capacity.

items.prompt: A Firehose stream delivers JSON records, but analysts need compressed Parquet partitioned for Athena. Which capability should be evaluated?

options.text: Use Firehose format conversion with an AWS Glue schema, compression, and S3 prefix design, then validate schema evolution, file size, and query pruning.
Store raw JSON only because Parquet cannot be created during ingestion.
Convert every record with a client Lambda and write one S3 object per event.
Use Global Accelerator to convert data formats at the edge.

feedback.Reason: Firehose can transform and convert supported record formats during delivery, improving analytical scan efficiency.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Format conversion uses a schema and batches data into columnar compressed files for S3 destinations.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner chooses buffer size and partitioning to avoid small files and validates the catalog and late records.
Details.errorCorrection: Parquet can be produced by supported conversion, one object per event is inefficient, and Global Accelerator is unrelated.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Conversion reduces query scan and storage cost but adds schema and transformation dependencies.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Supported conversion can produce columnar files during delivery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: One object per event creates small-file and request overhead.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Edge network services do not transform analytical record formats.

items.prompt: Several consumers need low-latency reads from the same Kinesis stream and one consumer currently affects the others. What should be evaluated?
constraints: The stream has multiple registered consumers.

options.text: Evaluate enhanced fan-out or another consumer-isolation pattern, comparing dedicated throughput, latency, registration limits, cost, and downstream capacity.
Use one shared polling loop for every consumer because reads are always isolated by the service.
Add more producer shards because consumer competition never depends on read throughput.
Disable retention so consumers cannot compete for older records.

feedback.Reason: Enhanced fan-out can provide dedicated read throughput and push delivery for registered consumers where shared polling is insufficient.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Kinesis consumer modes have different read-throughput sharing and delivery behavior; enhanced fan-out allocates dedicated consumer throughput per shard.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner evaluates consumer count, latency, cost, and downstream processing before selecting it.
Details.errorCorrection: Shared polling can compete, producer shards do not automatically solve read contention, and retention removal harms replay.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Dedicated fan-out improves isolation but adds consumer registration and cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Shared polling consumers can contend for read throughput.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Producer capacity and consumer read isolation are separate dimensions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Retention is needed for recovery and does not solve consumer bandwidth contention.

items.prompt: A team needs to move Kafka records to S3 without operating custom consumer code. Which integration should be evaluated?
constraints: Offset and failure behavior must be observable.

options.text: Evaluate Amazon MSK Connect or a managed Kafka connector, configuring worker capacity, connector offsets, networking, credentials, error handling, and S3 layout.
Use a DNS record to stream Kafka records into S3 without a consumer.
Use an S3 lifecycle policy as a Kafka connector.
Delete Kafka records after configuring the destination name, without validating delivery.

feedback.Reason: A Kafka connector provides a managed consumer and delivery path while preserving offset and connector operations.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: MSK Connect runs Kafka Connect workers and connectors that consume topics and deliver records to supported destinations.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect configures worker networking, IAM or secrets, scaling, offsets, retries, and error records.
Details.errorCorrection: DNS cannot consume records, lifecycle policies manage objects, and deleting source before delivery confirmation loses data.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Managed connectors reduce custom code but still require capacity, connector, offset, and failure operations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: DNS is not a data consumer or delivery connector.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 lifecycle manages stored objects, not Kafka records.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Source deletion must follow a verified delivery and retention contract.

items.prompt: A stream carries regulated records and keys must be controlled by the organization. What should be enabled?

options.text: Enable server-side encryption with an appropriate KMS key, configure key permissions and rotation, and validate producer, consumer, and recovery access over encrypted channels.
Use only client-side encryption and give every consumer the KMS administrator role.
Disable encryption because the stream is private to a VPC.
Store the KMS key in each record so consumers can decrypt it without IAM.

feedback.Reason: Managed stream encryption needs service, KMS, transport, and identity configuration rather than one broad role.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Kinesis and MSK expose encryption controls and use KMS or service-specific key behavior for data at rest and TLS for transit.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner limits key permissions, tests rotation and denied access, and keeps secrets out of payloads.
Details.errorCorrection: Client-only protection does not secure service copies, private networks are not encryption, and key material must never be put in records.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Customer-managed keys improve governance but add key availability and permission dependencies.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Broad KMS administrator access violates least privilege and does not configure service encryption.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Private network placement does not replace encryption at rest or in transit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Payloads must not contain raw key material.

items.prompt: A Kinesis stream is healthy but consumer iterator age grows during downstream database maintenance. What should the runbook do?
constraints: The backlog age has an RPO or freshness limit.

options.text: Monitor iterator age and retention headroom, pause or throttle consumers safely if needed, restore downstream capacity, and catch up with bounded concurrency before retention expires.
Delete the stream because a downstream outage makes retained records unusable.
Increase producer throughput to help the consumer catch up.
Reset offsets to the newest record without a loss decision or reconciliation plan.

feedback.Reason: A retained stream can absorb a downstream outage temporarily, but backlog age and retention define the recovery window.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Consumer lag grows while records remain available; recovery requires downstream capacity and a safe offset strategy.
Details.scenarioApplication: The operator protects retention, repairs the sink, and catches up idempotently while alarming on data age.
Details.errorCorrection: Deleting the stream destroys recovery, more input increases lag, and resetting to newest silently loses records.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Backlog recovery may consume downstream capacity and must be rate-limited to avoid a second outage.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Retention exists precisely to permit recovery from temporary consumer failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: More producer traffic worsens the backlog.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Offset reset is a data-loss decision and needs explicit approval and reconciliation.

items.prompt: Firehose delivers sensitive records to an S3 bucket owned by a central data account. Which access model should be used?
constraints: The bucket policy is centrally managed.

options.text: Grant the Firehose delivery role only the required bucket and prefix actions, align the cross-account bucket policy and KMS key policy, and test denied prefixes and rotation.
Grant the delivery role full S3 and KMS administration so delivery cannot fail.
Make the bucket public because Firehose writes are trusted by the service name.
Put the bucket credentials in each record so Firehose can authorize itself.

feedback.Reason: Cross-account delivery requires aligned role, bucket, and key permissions with least privilege.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Firehose assumes or uses a delivery role to write objects; S3 and KMS resource policies must allow that principal and required conditions.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner scopes prefixes and encryption keys and rehearses access denial and key rotation.
Details.errorCorrection: Full administration is excessive, public buckets expose data, and credentials must not be embedded in payloads.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Cross-account policy design adds coordination but supports centralized data ownership.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Delivery needs narrow write and encryption permissions, not administration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A service role does not make a bucket public-safe.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Payloads are not a secure credential channel.

items.prompt: A platform needs durable ordered events, replayable consumers, managed S3 delivery, and Kafka client compatibility for different workloads. What selection is correct?
constraints: Ordering and replay matter for some consumers.
Operations and cost must be explicit.

options.text: Use Kinesis Data Streams for partitioned replayable event consumption, Firehose for managed buffered delivery to destinations, and MSK when Kafka APIs and broker semantics are required.
Use Firehose for every workload because it provides unlimited replayable consumer groups and Kafka broker semantics.
Use MSK for every simple S3 delivery because managed Kafka removes all partition and broker decisions.
Use S3 alone as a streaming broker for ordered consumers and low-latency delivery.

feedback.Reason: Kinesis Data Streams, Firehose, and MSK have distinct ingestion, consumer, delivery, and operational models.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Streams expose partitioned retained records and consumers; Firehose buffers to destinations; MSK provides Kafka topics, brokers, partitions, and consumer groups.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect selects the smallest service model that satisfies ordering, replay, delivery, latency, and client compatibility.
Details.errorCorrection: Firehose is not a general consumer-group broker, MSK still needs Kafka operations, and S3 is durable storage rather than a low-latency broker.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Combining services can be correct, but each adds quotas, cost, security, and observability responsibilities.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Firehose does not provide arbitrary replayable consumer-group and Kafka broker semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: MSK retains substantial partition and broker design responsibility.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 lacks streaming broker ordering and low-latency consumer semantics.
